public_rationale: In a July–August 2026 survey of 637 US and UK researchers, respondents reported average time savings of almost seven hours weekly across scientific work [e1]. A separate preprint published on September 17, 2025 reported that experimental testing of AI-generated genomes yielded 16 viable phages [e2]. Together, the broad workflow reports and concrete experimental results support substantial practical assistance to human scientists and meet the early-resolution rule [e1, e2]. The survey study establishes associations, not a causal estimate of productivity gains [e3].
limitations: The workflow gains are self-reported by US and UK researchers; they do not establish universal benefits or a precise causal productivity effect [e1, e3].
Both supporting studies are preprints [e1, e2].
Verification costs and downstream experimental bottlenecks limit the reported benefits [e1].
The genome-design paper does not date each laboratory result within 2025 [e2].

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is substantial practical assistance to human-led scientific work, through saved effort or expanded research capabilities.
The analogy does not commit to matching a measured historical productivity gain from calculators or databases.
The sentence states no deadline and does not explicitly restrict assistance to systems built in 2026–2027.
Substantial benefits across documented research uses can settle this broad claim without proving gains for every scientist or field.
criteria.support_condition: Credible workflow evidence and documented scientific applications establish substantial practical gains for human scientists from AI assistance.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Broad, reliable evidence establishes that AI assistance provides no material practical gains across scientific work. Individual failures alone are insufficient.

evidence.explanation: The July–August survey of 637 US and UK researchers reports average savings of almost seven hours weekly across scientific work. These are self-reported gains, corroborated by the study’s broader evidence of scientific AI use.

evidence.publisher: bioRxiv; Samuel H. King and colleagues
evidence.explanation: Researchers report experimentally functional designs produced with genome language models. This supplies concrete evidence of expanded scientific capability alongside the broader workflow survey.

The authors caution against interpreting their results as causal productivity estimates. They also report verification burdens and downstream experimental bottlenecks, limiting stronger claims about the overall acceleration of science.

conclusive_event.meets_rule: The survey preprint became available on this date. Its reports of substantial assistance across scientific workflows, together with the experimental results already reported in e2, meet the rule requiring post-publication workflow evidence corroborated by concrete results in human-led research.
